messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Film Director
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Distraction: I distract myself with something else
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Vignette:
Nikolai Brennan is a 52-year-old film director of mixed Irish and Czech descent who presents for psychological assessment following a life-threatening road accident that occurred fourteen months ago. He lives with his long-term partner in Los Angeles, where he has worked in independent cinema for over two decades, building a reputation for visually meticulous, atmospherically dense films. He describes himself, prior to the accident, as someone who was in command — of a set, of a story, of himself.

The accident took place on a rain-slicked freeway at night. Nikolai was returning alone from a location scout when a truck drifted across the median and struck his car at speed. The vehicle spun, rolled, and came to rest on its roof in the dark. He remained conscious throughout, suspended by his seatbelt in near-total darkness, unable to move, unable to call for help, listening to the hiss of the engine and the sound of rain on crumpled metal. Emergency services took nearly forty minutes to reach him. He remembers the darkness most — not the impact, not the pain, but the dark and the sounds inside it, the way every creak of the chassis made him certain the car was about to collapse further.

In the weeks that followed, Nikolai found that what had happened to him seemed to resist language entirely. When his partner asked him to describe it, or when his therapist at the time gently encouraged him to put it into words, he found himself falling silent — not from unwillingness, but from a genuine incapacity. What he carried instead were images: the fractured geometry of the windshield, his own hands pressed flat against the roof of the upturned car, the red smear of tail lights visible through broken glass. These pictures arrived without invitation, vivid and complete, as if lit by a cinematographer he had not hired.

He had come to believe, in the months following the accident, that his responses to these images and to the world around him were evidence of something fundamentally broken in him. Other people, he was certain, would have moved on by now. The fact that he had not — that he still flinched when a car door slammed on a studio lot, that he still felt his chest seize when a grip dropped a lighting rig — seemed to him proof of a failure of character rather than the residue of trauma. He described himself in session as a lousy coper, and meant it without irony or self-pity, the way one states a professional assessment. The man who had directed twenty-three films, who had once prided himself on holding a crew's nerve during a difficult shoot, now startled at ordinary sounds that no one else seemed to notice. On set, this had consequences. A sound technician had commented, within earshot of others, that Nikolai seemed jumpy. He had not returned to that production.

He had also, quietly and then systematically, begun avoiding night shoots. His work had always depended on darkness — the long blue hours before dawn, the particular quality of artificial light against a night sky. He told his production company it was a scheduling preference. In truth, being in the dark had become something he could not reliably manage. The avoidance had narrowed the range of projects he could accept, and his partner, who had noticed the shift without fully understanding it, had begun to ask questions Nikolai did not know how to answer.

He spent considerable time trying to understand why this had happened to him — returning again and again to the question not as a spiritual inquiry but as a kind of compulsive audit, searching for the logic in it. He distracted himself with research, with reading, with the administrative work of development — anything that kept the images at bay for a few hours.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his partner, who told him, carefully and with evident love, that she no longer recognised him. The words landed with a precision that surprised him, because they matched exactly what he had been thinking about himself. He arrived at the intake appointment hoping, above all, to understand whether the person he had been before that night on the freeway still existed somewhere inside him, and afraid, in equal measure, that the answer might be no.
